The Annonaceae are a pantropical family largely confined to the warm, wet regions of the world with the notable exception of the genus Asimina Adans. which extends up through eastern North America to the Canadian border
The family consists of about 2300 species in some 132 genera
The family is well represented in Borneo with 35 genera as recognised in the current account
All of these have been recorded from Sabah and/or Sarawak and are represented by about 228 species across the two states, which include some 68 climbing species.
The Annonaceae are predominantly plants of the lowland tropical rain forest including swampy areas
While some species are found in montane forest, the family is certainly a characteristic lowland element in the floristics of tropical forest vegetation
There are species of Annonaceae found in the more seasonally dry parts of the tropics but they are less diverse than in the everwet regions.
In Borneo, the Annonaceae are an important element in lowland forests, both as trees and lianas
In an analysis of 28 forest plots across Borneo, Slik et al. (J. Biogeogr. 30 (2003) 1517--1531) found that the Annonaceae were represented in all the plots among trees of 9.8 cm dbh or larger
The family was ranked tenth in terms of abundance, averaging 3.2% of stems in each plot

The more limited data on lianas indicate that the Annonaceae are even better represented in both terms of abundance and diversity, generally in the top three with the legumes and palms (Putz & Chai, J. Ecol. 75 (1987) 523--531; Appanah et al., J. Trop
The enumeration of 52 ha of forest in the Lambir Hills NP in Sarawak (Lee et al., The 52-hectare Forest Research Plot at Lambir Hills, Sarawak, Malaysia
Sarawak, Kuching (2002) 1--621) is the most extensive data set on forest composition in Borneo
The large plot contains 54 species of Annonaceae among stems of 1 cm dbh or more

Interestingly, only four of these Annonaceae species (Goniothalamus velutinus, Phaeanthus macropodus (= a synonym of Phaeanthus ophthalmicus), Polyalthia cauliflora, Polyalthia insignis) failed to exceed 5 cm dbh, and only three attained the largest size class of >60 cm dbh (Maasia glauca, Mezzettia macrocarpa, Xylopia malayana); so the bulk are clearly midstorey and understorey species.
The family seems to occur in all forest habitats in Borneo except mangroves
Most species appear to be fairly wide-ranging

The number of narrow endemics is not great — examples include Orophea sarawakensis which is only known from G. Subis and Polyalthia montis-silam from G. Silam, and a suite of species from Mt. Kinabalu.

The lowland forests of Borneo are notable for having a reproductive phenology dominated by a strong supra-annual rhythmn that leads to irregular mast years when many trees produce flowers and fruits synchronously
At the Lambir Hills NP, where long-term phenological and pollination studies have been conducted, the Annonaceae demonstrated a range of different behaviours in terms of flowering phenology
Among eight Annonaceae species monitored over 53 months, six were observed in flower over this period, with four flowering annually or more frequently (Sakai et al., Amer

The common theme of pollination in the Annonaceae involves beetles within a pollination chamber (Momose in Roubik et al. (eds.), Pollination Ecology and the Rain Forest: Sarawak Studies, 174 (2005) 104--108)
The flowers are mostly bisexual and nearly always dichogamous, specifically protogynous, i.e. functionally female before being functionally male (Endress, Phil
The petals typically press closely over the reproductive structures forming a small chamber with restricted access between the petal margins

In species with free petals a complex process of petal movements may take place over time, forming and unforming the pollination chamber during the male and female phases of the flower, as demonstrated for Monoon coffeeoides (Thwaites ex Hook.f. & Thomson) B.Xue & R.M.K.Saunders and Hubera korinti (Dunal) Chaowasku in Sri Lanka by Ratnayake et al. (Intern
The beetles are attracted by scent and rewarded by various foods including stigmatic secretions and various flower structures, but apparently rarely by nectar, and sometimes by warmth

Thermogenesis has been detected in Annonaceae flowers with pollination chamber temperatures elevated by up to 8°C above ambient in Xylopia championii Hook.f. & Thomson in Sri Lanka (Ratnayake et al., Intern
The stamens may detach from the torus before they dehisce, sometimes being held by the spring-like thickenings of vascular bundles
This may facilitate access of the pollen to pollinators, as earlier the densely packed stamens with their relatively thick connectives helped protect the pollen from the pollinators
Beetles are the pre-eminent pollinators of Annonaceae
At the Lambir Hills NP, 20 of 22 species studied were beetle-pollinated – mostly Nitidulidae and Curculionidae (Momose et al., Amer
In Popowia pisocarpa, the small flowers have a very small pollination chamber, apparently restricting access to thrips (Momose et al., Biotropica 30 (1998) 444--448).

While protogyny may act to reduce self-pollination, it seems that some species have a fall-back mechanism where the stamens held on the extended vascular thickenings manage to contact the unfertilised stigmas that remain receptive leading to self-pollination
This has been demonstrated in Polyalthia littoralis (Blume) Boerl. = now a synonym of Monoon littorale (Blume) B.Xue & R.M.K.Saunders (Okada, Pl
A more subtle mechanism to promote xenogamy was uncovered by Rogstad (Amer
J. Bot. 81 (1994) 145--154) working on the reproductive biology of what are now considered species of Maasia
The temporal patterns of flower development were found to be highly synchronised on the same tree

In populations of Maasia hypoleuca and M. sumatrana at Pasoh, in Peninsular Malaysia, trees produced mature flowers at strict intervals of two days, but without exact synchrony across the whole population so that some trees had all female flowers on the same day as other trees has all male flowers and vice versa.
In general Annonaceae produce fruits with a pulpy flesh attractive to frugivorous animals
In Borneo, Annonaceae fruits have been recorded in the diets of a wide range of animals including orangutan, gibbon, sun-bear, tree-shrew species and many species of hornbill.
Despite being both diverse and often abundant the native Annonaceae of Borneo are relatively rarely used
The timber of Annonaceae is generally referred to as mempisang and contributes a relatively minor proportion of timber production in Borneo
While this proportion is likely to increase as the supply of preferred timbers declines, difficulties with taxonomy of the family hamper more detailed analysis.
There are reports of uses in traditional medicine particularly in species of Anaxagorea, Dasymaschalon, Goniothalamus, Phaeanthus and Polyalthia s.l
The best documented and scientifically supported medicinal application is for species of Phaeanthus which are used to treat sore eyes
Several species of Phaeanthus have been shown to contain quaternary and tertiary alkaloids that exhibit the property of reducing blood pressure and relaxing smooth muscle under laboratory conditions
Species of Goniothalamus contain various bioactive compounds
The various treelet species of Goniothalamus found in Borneo are generally referred to as limpanas or hujan panas
They have many traditional uses including repelling mosquitos, smoking-out bee nests and deterring poisonous snakes and evil spirits.
Several species of Annona and Stelechocarpus burahol are widely grown in gardens and kampung orchards for their edible fruits
A number of species are grown ornamentally, Polyalthia latifolia is grown as a street tree, mostly in the columnar form ‘Pendula’

Cananga odorata, while native, is also grown as a tree or shrub (var. fruticosa) for its fragrant blooms, though there is no evidence of it being grown commercially in Borneo for essential oil production as is done in the Philippines and Java

There seems little doubt that the Annonaceae represent a natural family, quite readily circumscribed and clearly allied to the Magnoliaceae and Myristicaceae in the order Magnoliales.
The most recent classification of the family (Chatrou et al., Bot
Soc. 169 (2012) 5--40), strongly based on molecular phylogenies, recognises four subfamilies
Subfamily Anaxagoreoideae, consisting solely of the genus Anaxagorea, is a sister group to the rest of the family

Subfamily Ambavioideae, including the genera Cananga, Cyathocalyx, Drepananthus and Mezzettia represented in Borneo, is in turn a sister group to the two largest subfamilies Annonoideae and Malmeoideae

In the Annonoideae, three tribes are represented in Borneo: Xylopieae (Artabotrys, Xylopia), Annoneae (Disepalum, Goniothalamus) and Uvarieae (Dasymaschalon, Desmos, Fissistigma, Friesodielsia, Mitrella, Pyramidanthe, Sphaerocoryne, Uvaria)

Similarly, in the Malmeoideae three tribes are represented in Borneo, the monogeneric Maasieae (Maasia) and Monocarpieae (Monocarpia), and the Miliuseae (Alphonsea, Hubera, Marsypopetalum, Meiogyne, Miliusa, Mitrephora, Monoon, Neo-uvaria, Orophea, Phaeanthus, Polyalthia s.s., Popowia, Pseuduvaria, Sageraea, Stelechocarpus and Trivalvaria).

Soc. 169 (2012) 5--40) in which elements once included in Polyalthia s.l. are spread over three different tribes.

The major fault line represents the splitting of the two traditionally recognised sections of the genus, i.e., sect. Polyalthia (often referred to as sect. Eupolyalthia in the old literature) and sect. Monoon
For Polyalthia s.l. sect. Monoon, this means the resurrection of the genus Monoon, but with the addition of the members of the genera Enicosanthum, Woodiellantha and Cleistopetalum
Also excised from Polyalthia s.l. are the species allied to Polyalthia sumatrana which are put in the genus Maasia, and the species allied to Polyalthia rumphii which are removed to Hubera.
Polyalthia s.s., as recognised here, is still a diverse and varied genus in Borneo

In Borneo recorded from Sabah (e.g., SAN 32098, SAN 83272 and SAN 127884), Sarawak (e.g., S 22364, S 33800, S 44944 and S 50588), Brunei (e.g., Sands MJS 5370) and Kalimantan (e.g., Kostermans 7532 and Kostermans 10243).
In Borneo G. ridleyi has been collected mostly from hill and montane forest at 750--3000 m altitude, but there are some collections from the lowlands, mostly described as swampy or riverine forest
This contrasts with G. ridleyi in the Peninsular Malaysia where it is largely a species of typical lowland rain forest.
Goniothalamus fasciculatus Boerl. was described from material from Borneo
Like G. ridleyi of the Peninsular Malaysia, it has many-flowered fascicles of large flowers on the tree trunk

While much of the Borneo material has smaller flowers with petals acute at the apex compared to the larger flowers and broad blunt petals of the Peninsular Malaysian material there are Borneo collections that do have more typical G. ridleyi type flowers
As outlined above, this may relate to an altitudinal variation in form among specimens
I therefore consider the Borneo material to belong in a more variable G. ridleyi and reduce G. fasciculatus to synonymy.
Sterile specimens of this species could conceivably be confused with Monocarpia but the basal inflorescences are highly distinctive.

Goniothalamus suaveolens has generally been considered an unpublished name and relegated to a dubious synonym of G. macrophyllus
The species was validly published by Beccari
It is clearly allied by its flower structure with G. parallelivenius
Goniothalamus parallelivenius is readily distinguished by the many-veined leaves

I therefore unite the elements which otherwise have very similar flowers and fruits

Some Bornean specimens have been determined as Monoon grandifolium (Elmer) B.Xue & R.M.K.Saunders (not to be confused with M. grandiflorum), a species from the Philippines

Certainly some specimens from the Philippines look similar to Bornean ones (SAN 37203 with slightly verrucose monocarps with distinct longitunal ridges seems similar to some specimens from Palawan), but M. grandifolium is typified by specimens with rounder monocarps covered with a pale tomentum

trait_value_raw: Only known in and around Kinabalu National Park in Sabah (e.g., G. Shea & Aban SAN 77174 (the type), Daim Andau 344, Daim Andau 855 and Daim Andau 1020).
Polyalthia lasioclada is similar to the widespread and rather variable Polyalthia microtus, particularly in flower form
The sepals of P. lasioclada are generally smaller than those of P. microtus (1--2 x 2--3 mm vs 4--6 x 4--6 mm)
The monocarps of P. lasioclada drying globose, relatively smooth and a golden brown whereas those of P. microtus are more cylindrical, drying with the surface minutely warty and a dark brown.
The villose twigs of Polyalthia lasioclada are similar to those of P. borneensis and P. bullata
However, these two species both have cream to yellow flowers with short villose pedicels rather than the orange-red flowers and relatively long, sparsely hairy pedicels of P. lasioclada
The many-veined leaves of P. bullata (25--40 pairs) are unlikely to be confused with P. lasioclada (15--19 pairs).

Boerlage (op. cit. 1899) compared this species to X. stenopetala when he described it
This is surprising as it shows little affinity to it except in the superficially similar leaf shape
Sinclair (op. cit. 1955) recognised the close link to X. malayana and reduced it to synonymy thereof
I have found little difficulty in separating X. mucronata from X. malayana – the mucronate leaves, dense reticulate venation and coriaceous petals of distinctive shape readily identify X. mucronata
I am therefore resurrecting this species.
